summary: A response to RFC 346 on satellite delays, from John Davidson at the University of Hawaii, which was due to join the ARPANET by satellite. He describes how the BCC 500 research group there was studying buffer allocation and partitioned echoing as ways to cope with long delays. It builds on design ideas from the BCC 500 communication system.

plainLanguage.summary: This response discusses how satellite delays can affect interactive computer use. It describes the University of Hawaii group's work on local echoing and the questions involved in adapting it to the ARPANET.

questions: how to handle long network delays
how can local echoing help with satellite delay
subtitle: A response on handling interactive sessions over long-delay satellite links.

tldr.problem: The University of Hawaii expected to join the ARPANET by satellite, where long delays could affect remote interactive use.
tldr.mechanism: The BCC 500 group was studying buffer allocation and partitioned echoing, in which a local concentrator could echo input while coordinating with the central computer.
tldr.outcome: The author describes unresolved questions about adapting these techniques to ARPANET and invites information about related work.

sections.title: The Satellite Delay Concern
sections.content:
The author says long transmission delays, such as those associated with satellite communication, concern users of remote interactive systems. The University of Hawaii expected to be linked to the ARPANET by satellite before the end of the year, making these consequences an immediate concern for the site.

The BCC 500 research group was studying buffer allocation, partitioned echoing and other problems raised in RFC 346.
sections.plainLanguage: A delayed response can make a remote interactive session difficult to use. Hawaii was preparing for a satellite connection and studying ways to handle that delay.

sections.title: Partitioned Echoing in BCC 500
sections.content:
The BCC 500 served geographically scattered users through remote concentrators. Its design allowed a concentrator to provide local echoing when appropriate, so a character could be shown at the terminal without waiting for the central computer's response.

A character input/output microprocessor and the user's process helped decide when local echoing was appropriate. The report says these coordination methods were not directly transferable to asynchronous ARPANET messages, especially with satellite delays.
sections.plainLanguage: A local concentrator can echo a typed character before the distant computer responds. The RFC says coordinating that local response with the central system is a problem for network messages.

sections.title: Where Echoing Might Be Handled
sections.content:
The author raises questions about whether local echoing should be handled by user TELNETs, by a TIP or by an IMP. If it were added at an IMP, the effect on a concentrator that already provides local echoing would need consideration.

The RFC says the effects on the existing network are not known and that the research group is seeking workable alternatives with the ILLIAC group at NASA-AMES. The author invites information about other work.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC does not settle where local echoing should be implemented. It asks how that choice would interact with existing systems and says the group is still studying alternatives.

references.text: RFC 346, which the response says raised related satellite-delay problems.
